extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, academics, and policymakers interested in computer- and electronics-related patent law
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly update summarizing recent and pending Supreme Court and Federal Circuit cases affecting patent law for computer and electronics technologies, highlighting substantive, procedural, and institutional standards. Useful as a survey of how courts are treating §101, §112, PTAB/IBR practice, standing, preclusion, claim construction, and separation-of-powers issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-Eligible Subject Matter (35 U.S.C. §101; Alice/Mayo two-step)
rubrics_metrics.description: What standard determines whether a patent claim is “directed to” a patent-ineligible concept under step 1 of the Supreme Court’s two-step Alice/Mayo framework; and whether patent eligibility (at each step of the Alice/Mayo framework) is a question of law for the court based on the scope of the claims or a question of fact for the jury based on the state of the art at the time of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Alice/Mayo two-step: (1) determine whether the claim is "directed to" a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., natural law); (2) if so, determine whether the claim recites an "inventive concept" sufficient to transform the ineligible concept into patent-eligible subject matter. Courts may treat the two steps differently (majority in American Axle found claims directed to Hooke’s law at step one and lacking an inventive concept at step two). Debates include whether courts improperly conflate enablement/§112 with §101, and whether eligibility is a pure question of law or involves factual inquiries (jury). The article notes splits at the Federal Circuit and Solicitor General interest (CVSG). Example/anti-pattern: treating §101 as a substitute for enablement leads to criticism that the court applied a "Nothing More" test that effectively imports §112 into §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-Plus-Function Claiming (§112(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-step means-plus-function analysis: (1) determine whether a claim limitation is drafted in means-plus-function format; (2) if yes, determine what structure, if any, the specification discloses corresponding to the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For step one, consider presence of the word "means," whether the term would be understood by a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) as the name for a structure, intrinsic evidence (claims, prosecution history), and extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, expert testimony). If claim does not recite "means," the challenger bears the burden (preponderance of the evidence) to show the limitation fails to recite sufficiently definite structure. A class of structures may suffice (single specific structure not required). Examples from Federal Circuit precedent: "circuit" can connote structure; "user identification module" may not. For software terms (e.g., "code"/"application"), structure may be defined in part by function and by reference to algorithms—absence of algorithmic disclosure can render a claim indefinite. In Dyfan v. Target the court looked to expert testimony and claim context to conclude "code"/"application" connote structure and the "system" limitation was defined by the claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description / Corresponding-Structure Requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must disclose corresponding structure for functional claim elements (including means-plus-function claims); failure to disclose corresponding structure or algorithm (for software-implemented functions) can render claims indefinite under §112(b) or otherwise fail written description/enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When §112(f) applies, courts examine whether the specification provides adequate corresponding structure (for software, algorithms are often the required structure). District court in Dyfan found no algorithm and held claims indefinite; Federal Circuit reversed on step one but highlighted that absence of corresponding structure is a separate problem. The article highlights the interplay and potential confusion between §112 (enablement/written description) and §101 analyses, including criticisms that courts may incorrectly collapse these requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preclusion under the Kessler Doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether Kessler v. Eldred creates a freestanding preclusion doctrine barring litigation against customers of a prior prevailing party even when claim or issue preclusion do not apply; and whether Kessler can extend to cases where the prior judgment was a voluntary dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kessler bars a patent infringement suit against a customer of a seller who previously prevailed against a patentee on related claims. Key fact patterns include prior voluntary dismissals and subsequent suits against customers. The PersonalWeb v. Patreon litigation raised (1) whether the Federal Circuit correctly interpreted Kessler as freestanding preclusion and (2) whether Kessler applies where the prior proceedings were voluntarily dismissed; Federal Circuit applied Kessler to preclude customer suits, and the petitioners argued this was error. Guidance: analyze the preclusive effect of prior judgments on downstream suits, paying close attention to the nature of the prior disposition (judgment vs voluntary dismissal) and traditional claim/issue preclusion principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate Review of Patent Jury Verdicts and Claim Construction (O2 Micro duty; Seventh Amendment limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an appellate court may reverse a jury verdict by sua sponte adopting a new claim construction where the district court declined to construe the term (treating it as plain and ordinary meaning) and the jury resolved infringement facts; and the duty of a district court to resolve fundamental claim term disputes (O2 Micro).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parties present a fundamental dispute about claim scope, O2 Micro requires the court to construe the term rather than leaving it to the jury; appellate courts must be cautious about recasting factual issues as claim construction issues post hoc. Olaf Sööt Design v. Daktronics exemplifies the issue where the Federal Circuit's sua sponte construction recast a jury factual finding as a legal issue, leading to reversal. Guidance: ensure district courts resolve claim term disputes to avoid improper jury submissions; appellate reversal based on new constructions risks Seventh Amendment concerns if it effectively supplants the jury's factfinding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article III Standing to Appeal PTAB IPR Decisions (licensee standing; MedImmune)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a licensee (particularly under a multi-patent/portfolio license) has Article III standing to appeal a PTAB final written decision invalidating some patents covered by a license agreement; interaction with MedImmune's holding on licensee standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the licensee has alleged a concrete injury in fact and redressability sufficient for Article III standing (MedImmune recognizes licensees can have standing where ongoing obligations are affected). In Apple v. Qualcomm the Federal Circuit held Apple lacked Article III standing because Apple had not alleged the validity of the patents at issue would affect its contractual obligations (ongoing royalty obligations). Guidance: distinguish single-patent licenses from portfolio licenses; evaluate evidence of ongoing concrete harm or alteration of contractual rights to establish standing to appeal IPR outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and Permissible Evidence in PTAB Trials (expert testimony; interpretation vs gap-filling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether petitioners in IPR may rely on expert testimony to "fill in gaps" in the prior art when asserting unpatentability, or whether expert testimony is limited to illustrating/interpreting admissible prior art; and broader admissibility questions for PTAB fact-finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baxter v. Becton, Dickinson raised whether the PTAB improperly permitted expert testimony to supply missing elements not disclosed in prior art (petitioners' characterization) versus using experts only to interpret what prior art would have taught a PHOSITA. Parties dispute the characterization; guidance is to scrutinize whether expert testimony merely explains or improperly supplies missing technical content. Also consider how the Board treats expert evidence and whether appellate review should defer to PTAB factual findings (substantial evidence) versus legal conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Limits on Inter Partes Review (AIA §311(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner in an inter partes review may request cancellation of claims only on grounds that could be raised under §102 or §103 and only on the basis of prior art consisting of patents or printed publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPR petitions must be grounded solely on novelty/obviousness under §§102/103 and rely only on patents/printed publications as prior art; other grounds or types of evidence are outside the statutory scope. This statutory constraint frames what the PTAB may consider and what expert testimony may legitimately interpret. Practitioners should ensure challenges are framed within these statutory boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-Agency Separation of Powers and the Ordinary Remand Rule (Chenery doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the Federal Circuit resolving contested patentability issues on appeal (on grounds the PTAB did not consider) rather than remanding to the agency for initial decision violates the Chenery principle that a reviewing court should judge agency action only on the grounds the agency invoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baxter argued that the Federal Circuit's resolution of patentability on different grounds than the Board's decision runs afoul of Chenery and separation-of-powers concerns, and that contested issues should be remanded to the PTAB to decide in the first instance. Becton, Dickinson responded that appellate courts have power to review legal standards de novo and factual determinations for substantial evidence. Guidance: when appealing PTAB decisions, consider whether appellate courts are addressing issues the Board actually decided or substituting their own determinations; careful invocation of Chenery may require remand where the Board did not pass on a contested ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Construction and Related Doctrines (prosecution disclaimer; effect on damages; grammar of claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various claim-construction principles affecting infringement, damages, and related evidentiary rulings: prosecution disclaimer's effect on limiting claim scope; how claim construction can affect damages calculations and admissibility of expert testimony on damages; and textual/grammatical issues (e.g., construing "and" to mean "or").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction can have cascading effects beyond infringement: it can trigger prosecution disclaimer, alter damages assessments, and affect what expert testimony is admissible. The article cites cases addressing prosecution disclaimer, the effect of claim construction on damages and expert admissibility (Apple v. Wi-LAN), and interpretive choices like reading "and" as "or" (Michael Kaufman v. Microsoft). Guidance: analyze intrinsic evidence/prosecution history for disclaimer; anticipate how narrowing or broadening constructions influence damages and expert opinions; be mindful that ordinary grammatical cues may be overridden by technical context or prosecution history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness as a Legal Determination and Appellate Review Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is ultimately a legal determination (based on underlying factual findings), and appellate review may assess legal conclusions de novo while deferring to factual findings for substantial evidence; KSR provides guidance on obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts recognize obviousness involves mixed questions: underlying factual findings (e.g., scope and content of prior art, differences, level of ordinary skill) are reviewed for substantial evidence, while the ultimate legal determination may be reviewed de novo. Parties and courts will cite KSR and subsequent Federal Circuit/CAFC precedent when framing obviousness arguments; below-article cases (e.g., Baxter) raised whether appellate courts' handling of obviousness on new grounds is appropriate or whether remand to the agency is required.
